How can we read a molecule?
Molecules are not motionless.
Some vibrations can couple to infrared light.
Molecules leave their own clues in infrared light.
How can we read those clues?
Different vibrations absorb infrared light at different frequencies.
The remaining component strengths carry clues about the sample.
Yet the detector gives just one total response.
Change the sample, and the absorption pattern changes.
The total amount of remaining light can still be the same.
The total alone cannot tell us which components were absorbed.
What if we took more than one reading?
We deliberately change the measurement conditions
and observe how the total response changes.
Split the light into two paths, reflect it back, and let it meet again.
Both paths contain the original broadband components.
This arrangement is a Michelson interferometer.
Now move one of the mirrors.
When the mirror moves, light travels the extra distance twice.
The added path is twice the mirror displacement.
The difference between the two paths is the optical path difference.
When the waves meet again, their alignment has changed.
Aligned waves reinforce each other; displaced waves can cancel.
This relative offset is called a phase difference.
As the mirror moves continuously, the output intensity varies.
Do different wavenumbers vary in the same way?
Continue moving the mirror with the same scan.
One has completed three bright–dark cycles; the other, only one.
In one scan, different wavenumbers leave different rhythms.
The mirror changes the path difference, not the component wavenumbers.
Use the same scan to compare the two samples again.
The samples gave the same single reading, but their scan records differ.
The combined rhythms still shape the total signal.
Follow the recombined light and look at sample A again.
Follow one component and observe what changes.
Its variation becomes smaller.
Its wavenumber and rhythm remain unchanged.
The sample reduces its contribution to the total signal.
Keep the sample unchanged and complete a scan.
At each scan position, the detector records one total response.
This scan record is called an interferogram.
It records how the total response varies with path difference.
To isolate the variation, subtract the constant baseline.
Above and below zero mean changes relative to that baseline.
All the rhythms are mixed here. How strong is each one?
Test the record with a curve of known rhythm.
We call it a probe.
Multiply the record and probe at the same positions.
Matching signs give positive contributions; opposite signs give negative ones.
Accumulate these contributions along the scan.
Here, positive and negative contributions cancel repeatedly.
By the end, the accumulated result is nearly zero.
Tune the probe to another rhythm and try again.
The matching component rises and falls together with the probe.
Their product therefore gives positive contributions.
Contributions from other rhythms tend to cancel.
The accumulation still fluctuates, but leaves a clear net result.
How much remains at the end
reflects the strength of that rhythm in the record.
Place the result at its corresponding wavenumber.
Repeat with different rhythms.
The strength of each wavenumber component gradually appears.
The component weakened by the sample is also lower here.
This is what the Fourier transform does here.
But how strong should this component have been?
Was it weakened by the sample, or by the source and instrument?
First scan and record the background without the sample.
Then insert the sample and scan under the same conditions.
Fourier-transform the two records separately.
This gives the background and sample spectra.
At each wavenumber, divide the sample result by the background.
The ratio tells us how much remains relative to the background.
It is called transmittance.
Lower transmittance means more light was attenuated in that region.
We can also convert it to absorbance.
Here, stronger absorption gives a higher peak.
The earlier components were synthetic.
Now we switch to an illustrative chemical absorption example.
This band, for example, suggests carbon–oxygen double-bond stretching.
The molecular environment also affects the band position.
One peak is not enough to identify a molecule.
Other absorption features must be considered together.
From changes in total response, we recover the sample spectrum.
Molecular motion has left recognizable clues.
